newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberian poll winner extends olive branch.
newsitem.headline: Liberian poll winner extends olive branch.

text.p: The winner of Liberia's presidential election, ex-warlord Charles Taylor, extended an olive branch to rivals before the formal proclamation of his victory on Thursday.
Taylor told BBC radio he was ready to offer jobs to some of his 11 rivals in Saturday's presidential and general elections, wrapping up an accord ending seven years of civil war.
Two rival faction leaders in the war vied with Taylor, but he specifically mentioned the runner-up in the poll, former United Nations executive Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf.
"I will offer some of them senior positions and others junior positions. We must go together," Taylor said.
"I intend to use the talents of most of the fellows that I have respect for, including Ellen," he said.
It was Taylor's first interview since partial official results on Tuesday showed him with an unassailable lead of more than 75 percent of votes cast.
Taylor was being formally proclaimed elected by the elections commission later on Thursday.
Four rival candidates have conceded defeat to Taylor. Three others -- Johnson-Sirleaf and ex-warlords Alhaji Kromah and George Boley -- have alleged polling day irregularities.
None has yet rejected the election, declared free and fair by more than 500 international observers and over 1,000 local monitors.
"I have received letters from two political parties and listened to two others on the radio. They have expressed their willingness to do whatever they are asked to do," Taylor said.
"This is a very small country that had a very terrible war," Taylor said of the need for reconciliation.
A source close to the commission told Reuters Taylor's final victory margin could be between 80 and 85 percent.
In the results issued on Tuesday, Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the presidential race, took 9.5 percent of votes.
No other candidate attained five percent, prompting Johnson- Sirleaf to declare Taylor's margin of victory as "statistically impossible".
But despite renewing charges of polling day irregularities, Johnson-Sirleaf would accept the election results, a close political associate of the former U.N. executive told Reuters.

"She is going to make a new statement after the proclamation of the results," the associate said. "She will offer her party's readiness to participate in Taylor's government, although she herself will not play a role in it."
On Wednesday ,Taylor rivals Cletus Wortorson and Baccus Mathews conceded victory to Taylor in a move that has vastly diminished strong fear of post-poll trouble.
"Results of the elections announced so far show that the Liberian people overwhelmingly decided that Taylor should be the president of Liberia," Wortorson told reporters.
Wortoson, 60, came fourth with 2.5 percent of votes in the latest partial results.
"We congratulate Mr Taylor," Wortorson said, calling on his Alliance of Political Parties supporters to back Taylor.
Mathews, a former foreign minister, also endorsed the elections as "reasonably free and fair". He called on Taylor's other rivals alleging malpractice to accept the outcome.
"There were problems but they were not massive enough to affect the result," Mathews told Reuters.
Taylor needed 50 percent plus to win on the first round.
Liberians looking for strong leadership after the devastating civil war voted overwhelmingly for Taylor, the man who started the fighting in December 1989.
Liberia was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first modern republic.
